newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel passes bill that saves arts endowment.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel passes bill that saves arts endowment.

text.p: A Senate panel on Friday approved a $13 billion spending bill that would save the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) and buy land to protect Yellowstone National Park and a tract of ancient trees in California.

Seeking to avoid a confrontation with the White House, the Senate Interior Appropriations subcommittee included those priorities of President Bill Clinton's that the House of Representatives dropped from its bill that passed earlier this week.

"I hope we can find a way to get some bi-partisan support that will carry over to the House" and save the NEA to avoid a White House veto of the final bill, Alaska Republican Ted Stevens, chairman of the full Appropriations Committee, said.

The House, after a drawn-out floor fight, wiped out funding for the arts agency that gives grants to community orchestras, theatres, film-makers and other artists. But the Senate panel's bill would keep the agency's funding for next fiscal year at this year's $100 million level.

"This is a very good day for the arts endowment. One hundred million dollars is a strong endorsement by the Senate subcommittee and a clear signal of broad bipartisan support for the NEA," NEA chairwoman Jane Alexander said in a statement.
The interior bill covers spending for a range of programmes for federal lands, Native Americans, energy research and security, minerals management and culture.

Unlike the House bill, the Senate panel's bill would use $700 million from a Land and Water Conservation Fund to buy public lands, including $65 million to pay a company not to develop a gold mine on the edge of Yellowstone National Park, and $250 million to save the Headwaters grove in California, the nation's largest remaining uncut old-growth forest.
However, spending to block the mine and save the tract of ancient trees first would have to be approved by the Senate Energy Committee.

Of the remaining $385 million, $100 million would be used for state acquisitions and $285 million would be used over four years to buy land according to priorities to be set later by Congress and the White House. The White House opposes use of the funds for state land purchases.

The bill provides an $80 million increase for the National Parks Service for one percent across-the-board spending increases to all parks and other improvements, as well as additional money for equipment and other projects.

It meets the White House request to spend $757.4 million on programmes for Native Americans, up $76.5 million over this year, and funds energy research and development at $364 million, near this year's level.
To leave room for some of the spending increases, the bill would sell $207.5 million of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to cover the reserve's operating costs.
The administration has said it opposes the sale. Subcommittee Chairman Slade Gorton said he would be willing to try to find ways to avoid it, but said it would be difficult.
